opus-5.5.text:
I like that analogy, because it changes how you think about the whole stack. If tokens are like electricity, then inference infrastructure is the power grid, and the model architecture is the power plant. Most of the cost of electricity isn't only in generation. It's also in transmission, in balancing supply and demand, in how efficiently you can deliver it to where it's needed. Tokens work the same way.

In the early days, people designed models almost purely for quality. Make the benchmark go up, and inference was someone else's problem. Then the infra people, like those of us working on vLLM, would receive the model and try to serve it as cheaply and quickly as possible. That's like building a power plant without thinking about the grid. It produces energy, but maybe at a voltage or rhythm that's very expensive to transmit.

Co-design means the architecture people and the infrastructure people sit at the same table from the start. A good example is attention and the KV cache. During decoding, the bottleneck often isn't compute but memory: how much KV cache you have to store and move for every token. So architectural choices like grouped-query attention, multi-head latent attention, sliding windows, or hybrid designs with linear attention or state-space layers are really decisions about the cost of transmitting electricity. They shrink what you have to carry around per token.

Mixture-of-experts is another one. On paper it gives you a huge model with low active compute. But in serving, it raises questions like how to place experts across GPUs, how to handle all-to-all communication, and how to keep load balanced so some GPUs aren't idle while others are overloaded. If the model designer ignores that, the theoretical savings disappear in practice. If they design with it in mind, choosing the number of experts or routing behavior to fit the hardware topology, you get real cheaper tokens.

The same goes for things like speculative decoding or multi-token prediction. If the model is trained with a built-in draft head, the inference engine can generate several tokens per step. That's like the plant and the grid agreeing on a protocol that makes delivery more efficient.

So the core idea is this: what users ultimately pay for is cost per useful token at a certain latency. You can't optimize that from only one side. Model architecture decides what the workload looks like, and infrastructure decides how efficiently that workload runs on real hardware. When tokens become a utility consumed at massive scale, like electricity, even a small per-token efficiency gain is worth enormous amounts of money. That's why I think co-design isn't just a nice-to-have anymore. It's becoming the main way the industry drives the price of intelligence down.

r001.rationale: The response compares model architecture to a power plant and discusses fitting design choices to hardware, but it does not connect the plant’s design to an available natural energy resource.

r002.rationale: It compares inference infrastructure to a power grid and describes delivering tokens efficiently to where they are needed, matching distribution of electricity to consumers.

fable-5.1.text:
I like this analogy because it changes what you think the product is. When people talk about AI, they usually picture a model, a brain in a box. But from where I sit, working on inference, what we actually deliver is tokens. Tokens are the thing that flows out and does work in the world. And in that sense tokens are a lot like electricity.

Think about what electricity needed before it was useful. It wasn't enough to invent a generator. You needed a grid, you needed transformers, you needed standards for voltage and frequency, you needed a way to meter it and bill for it. And crucially, the generator and the grid shaped each other. We ended up with alternating current not because it was the most elegant physics, but because it transmitted efficiently over long distances through the infrastructure people could actually build. The generation side adapted to the transmission side, and vice versa.

Model architecture and inference infrastructure are in exactly that relationship right now. The model is the power plant. The serving system, things like vLLM, the GPU clusters, the scheduling, the memory management, that's the grid. If you design the plant without thinking about the grid, you get a model that's wonderful in a paper and painful to serve. And if you design the grid without understanding how plants are changing, you build for yesterday's models.

Let me give concrete examples. The KV cache is the clearest one. Attention makes every new token look back at every previous token, so you keep that history in GPU memory. On the infrastructure side, we spent a lot of effort making that memory management efficient, paging it, sharing it across requests with the same prefix. But then architecture people looked at the same bottleneck and said, what if we just need less of it? So you get multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, and DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention, which compresses the cache. That's a model design decision made entirely because of what it costs to serve. The grid told the plant how to generate.

It goes the other direction too. Mixture of experts is an architecture choice, only a fraction of parameters activate per token. That sounds free until you serve it. Now you need expert parallelism, you need to route tokens across GPUs, you need to handle load imbalance when everyone's tokens want the same expert. The infrastructure had to be rebuilt around it. Speculative decoding is another, you need a draft model and a verify step, and the scheduler has to understand that.

So co-design just means: stop pretending there's a clean handoff. In the electricity world, nobody builds a plant and then hopes a grid shows up. The people designing the model and the people designing the serving stack should sit in the same room, because the cost per token, the latency per token, the throughput per GPU, those numbers are determined jointly. Neither side owns them.

And the reason this matters commercially is the same reason it mattered for electricity. Once tokens become a utility, the competition isn't about who has a plant. Everyone has a plant. It becomes about who delivers reliably at the lowest cost per unit. That's an infrastructure problem and an architecture problem at the same time, and the teams that treat it as one problem will win.

r001.rationale: The response says model architecture adapts to serving constraints such as KV-cache costs, but it does not compare that adaptation to designing a generator for an available natural energy resource.

r002.rationale: It compares the serving system to an electricity grid and says tokens flow out, but does not clearly state that the inference engine delivers tokens to users as a power system distributes electricity to households.

astra-6.text:
I think of tokens as electricity: users want a useful output, but behind that output there is an entire system that produces and delivers it. The model is like the power plant, and the inference infrastructure is like the grid. You have to design them together, because the cost of producing something and the cost of delivering it are connected.

For example, an architecture might look very efficient if you just count its arithmetic operations. But if running it requires moving a lot of data between GPUs, or keeping a huge amount of memory for each conversation, it may actually be slow and expensive to serve. It’s like building an efficient power plant somewhere that makes transmission very difficult.

Co-design means bringing those constraints into the architecture decisions, and then building the inference system to exploit the architecture. How much computation do we need per token? How much memory? How much communication? Can we batch requests efficiently while still responding quickly?

And tokens aren’t quite interchangeable units of electricity. A cheaper token isn’t necessarily a better result if the model needs many more tokens to solve the task. So the goal is really to deliver useful intelligence at a good cost and latency, with the model and infrastructure working together.

r001.rationale: It says architecture and inference infrastructure should be designed together and mentions GPU movement, memory, and communication, but it does not describe adapting the architecture to hardware characteristics as designing a generator for an available natural energy resource.

r002.rationale: It compares the model to a power plant and inference infrastructure to the grid, describing the grid as delivering the model’s output, which conveys a power system distributing tokens to users.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of tokens as electricity: the model generates them, and the inference infrastructure delivers them. What matters to the user is whether those tokens arrive quickly, reliably, and at a reasonable cost.

Co-design means you don’t design the power plant independently of the grid. A model architecture determines the computation, memory, and communication needed to produce each token. The inference system determines how efficiently we can execute that work on actual hardware.

For example, an architecture might look very efficient if you count only arithmetic operations, but if it requires moving a lot of data between devices, it can still be slow in practice. So we need a feedback loop: infrastructure constraints inform the architecture, and architectural choices inform the kernels, scheduling, and deployment strategy. The goal is to deliver useful tokens efficiently while preserving model quality.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware and infrastructure constraints should inform architecture, but it does not communicate designing a generator around an available natural energy resource.

r002.rationale: It says the inference infrastructure delivers tokens to users and compares co-design to a power plant and grid, conveying the analogy of delivering electricity through a power system.
